title: The Queen of Sheba and Solomon's Splendor
summary: The queen of Sheba comes to Jerusalem with a great caravan to test Solomon with hard questions. Overwhelmed by his wisdom, his court, and his worship, she blesses the LORD who set Solomon on His throne to do justice and righteousness, and exchanges lavish gifts with him. The chapter then describes Solomon's gold, his golden shields, his ivory throne, his fleets, and the kings of the earth who sought his wisdom, and it closes with his forty-year reign and death.
story: This chapter is the summit and the end of Solomon's story in Chronicles. The wisdom God gave at Gibeon (chapter 1) is now known across the world, and a foreign queen confesses that Israel's God is its source. The promise of riches and honor in 1:12 has been fulfilled beyond measure. Then, abruptly, Solomon dies and Rehoboam reigns. The Chronicler does not tell the story of Solomon's later idolatry, his many foreign wives, or the adversaries God raised against him, all told in 1 Kings 11. Chapter 10 will show the kingdom splitting under his son, and the reader who knows Kings will hear the unspoken reasons.
historical:
The chapter follows 1 Kings 10:1-29 closely and adds the concluding notice of verses 29-31. Sheba is generally identified with Saba, a kingdom in southwestern Arabia (modern Yemen), known from its own inscriptions and famous in antiquity for frankincense, myrrh, and spices carried north by camel caravan along the incense routes. Sabaean inscriptions naming the kingdom and its rulers are mostly later than Solomon's time, and no queen of Sheba is named in any surviving inscription, so the visit is known only from the Bible and later traditions built on it. Ethiopian tradition, preserved in the medieval Kebra Nagast, holds that she bore Solomon a son, Menelik, founder of Ethiopia's royal line; this is a later legend, not part of the biblical account.

Verse 29 cites three prophetic sources for Solomon's reign: records of Nathan, a prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite (who appears in 1 Kings 11 foretelling the division of the kingdom), and visions of Iddo the seer. None has survived. "Ships of Tarshish" (verse 21) probably refers to a class of large seagoing vessels, named after a distant port (often located in Spain), rather than ships that literally sailed to Tarshish from the Red Sea.
cultural:
Visits between rulers, with exchanges of rich gifts, were a regular part of ancient diplomacy, and they often had commercial purposes. The queen's caravan of spices, gold, and precious stones may also reflect trade negotiations, since Solomon's control of routes through Israel and his fleet on the Red Sea touched Arabian commerce. Testing a ruler with riddles or hard questions was a known form of contest in the ancient world; wisdom was a mark of royal legitimacy.

The ivory throne with six steps and lions (verses 17-19) was a statement of royal power; lions were widely used as royal and divine symbols in the Near East, and ivory-inlaid furniture has been found in Assyrian palaces and at Samaria. The golden shields were ceremonial, displayed in the House of the Forest of Lebanon, a great hall named for its rows of cedar pillars. They would not last: Shishak of Egypt carried them off in the next generation (12:9). The creatures in verse 21 are uncertain; the Hebrew words translated "apes and peacocks" may also mean baboons or other monkeys.
literary: The chapter has two parts: the queen's visit (verses 1-12) and a catalog of Solomon's wealth and fame (13-28), followed by the formal closing of his reign (29-31). The queen's speech (5-8) is the theological center, and the Chronicler shapes it to his own themes: where 1 Kings 10:9 says God set Solomon on the throne of Israel, Chronicles says God set him “on His throne to be king for the LORD your God” (verse 8). The catalog is built from superlatives: nothing too difficult, never such spices, nothing like this ever made, surpassed all the kings of the earth. Verses 25-28 repeat almost exactly 1:14-17, so that Solomon's story is framed by the same picture of wealth at its start and its end.

outline.t: The queen of Sheba comes to test Solomon
Gifts exchanged, and algum wood from Ophir
Solomon's gold, shields, throne, and fleet
The kings of the earth seek Solomon's wisdom
Solomon's death and the record of his reign

doctrines.note: Solomon's wisdom, God's gift in chapter 1, draws the nations. The kings of the earth come "to hear the wisdom that God had put in his heart" (verse 23). Wisdom is presented not as Solomon's achievement but as God's gift displayed to the world.

The queen confesses that God set Solomon on His throne to be king for the LORD, and that the purpose of his reign was "to carry out justice and righteousness" (verse 8). The king's wealth exists for the sake of just rule, and the kingdom is ultimately God's.

A foreign ruler hears of Israel's God through the fame of his king and blesses him. This is the fulfillment, in a small way, of Solomon's prayer that foreigners would come because of God's great name (6:32-33).

words.note: Chidah, riddle or hard question. The queen comes to test Solomon with chidot (verse 1). The same word is used for Samson's riddle (Judges 14) and for the dark sayings of wisdom (Proverbs 1:6). It suggests a probing contest of wit and insight.

Esher, blessed or happy, the word that opens Psalm 1. The queen uses it twice: how blessed are your men, how blessed your servants who hear your wisdom (verse 7). It describes the fortunate condition of those who live near wisdom.

Mishpat, justice, often paired with tsedaqah, righteousness, as in verse 8. The pair describes the heart of the king's calling in the Old Testament: to rule fairly, protect the weak, and uphold what is right. The queen names it as the reason God gave Israel a king.

Kisse, throne. Solomon sits on an ivory throne of gold (verses 17-19), but the queen says God set him on "His throne" (verse 8). The Chronicler consistently presents the Davidic throne as God's own, held by the king in trust.

christ: Jesus himself drew on this chapter. He said that the queen of the South came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon's wisdom, and that something greater than Solomon was now present (Matthew 12:42; Luke 11:31). She traveled far for Solomon; his hearers would not listen to one who stood among them. The chapter's picture of nations bringing gold and spices to a son of David is echoed in the psalms and prophets: Psalm 72 prays that the kings of Sheba will bring gifts to the king, and Isaiah 60:6 pictures those from Sheba bringing gold and frankincense to Jerusalem. Matthew's account of the magi bringing gold, frankincense, and myrrh to the infant Jesus (Matthew 2:11) draws on this imagery, though Matthew doesn't cite this chapter. The link is thematic: the nations who came to Solomon's wisdom anticipate the nations who come to Christ.

hard.q: Why does the Chronicler leave out Solomon's fall into idolatry?
hard.a:
First Kings 11 tells how Solomon's many foreign wives turned his heart to other gods in his old age, how God raised adversaries against him, and how God announced that the kingdom would be torn from his son. Chronicles omits all of this and ends Solomon's reign at the height of its glory. Some readers see this as whitewashing.

Most interpreters see instead a deliberate focus. The Chronicler knew his readers had the books of Kings; he does not deny Solomon's sins, and he even alludes to them by citing Ahijah's prophecy in verse 29 and by opening chapter 10 with the consequences. His purpose was to present David and Solomon together as the founders of the temple and its worship, the model of what Israel's life with God should be, for a community rebuilding that worship. Others note that the details of Solomon's excess in this chapter (horses from Egypt, heaps of gold and silver) are exactly what Deuteronomy 17:16-17 warned a king against, so the attentive reader can see the danger even here. Both readings take the text seriously: it celebrates what God gave while leaving the shadow in plain view for those who know the rest of the story.

questions: The queen said she didn't believe the reports until she saw with her own eyes. What would someone see in your life or church that makes the reports about God believable?
The queen said God made Solomon king to carry out justice and righteousness. How should wealth and power be measured by that purpose?
Jesus said someone greater than Solomon was present. What would it mean to seek his wisdom with the queen's effort and eagerness?
